title: Clean Code
description: Study the complete supplied 67-page excerpt: care, maintenance, precise requirements, clean-code judgment, authorship and small refactorings. Guided practice and quizzes accompany a full page-ordered text reference.

children.title: Your learning path and source scope

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Recognize what this excerpt actually contains and choose a short, active study session.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 1–67. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: What is available
slides.body:
This is the 67-page excerpt supplied for this course. It contains publication material and contents (PDF 1–18), James O. Coplien’s foreword (19–23), the introduction and acknowledgments (25–28), On the Cover (29), Chapter 1 Clean Code (31–45), the book index (47–65), and publisher registration and subscription offers (66–67). Pages 6, 18, 24, 30 and 46 contain intentional-blank notices.

Later chapters are named in the contents and index but their actual explanations and case studies are absent. An index entry is a pointer, not a lesson from that missing chapter.

slides.title: How the lessons work
slides.body:
Modules 02–06 explain every substantive topic present in the foreword, introduction and Chapter 1. Each lesson has an objective, a focused explanation, a practice task and a worked check. Module 07 applies these ideas in an original JavaScript refactoring clinic. Module 08 preserves ALL extracted text, including credits, contents, index entries, footnotes and advertisements, in original page order.

Original examples are labeled as course exercises. They are not listings from the book. The site does not run arbitrary code; use your own console or project.

slides.title: Choose a manageable session
slides.body:
Read one lesson, stop at Practice, and write your own explanation before revealing the worked check. In five to ten minutes you can improve one name, one boundary or one test. Then take the relevant module quiz.

Use lesson notes for a Feynman explanation: What is this idea? Why does it matter? What example shows it? What part can I not explain yet?

slides.title: Progress and copying
slides.body:
All lessons and quizzes are open by default. Reports, notes and completion save only in this browser. Quizzes are study feedback, not secure exams. Passing is 80% and retakes are available.

Copy entire course includes explanations, every source page, practice, answer choices and worked answers. It excludes your notes and progress. Settings can enable completion gates; with gates enabled, reference decks also count as lessons.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Find Chapter 1 and the full source reference in the outline. Name two topics this excerpt can teach and one later chapter it cannot reproduce.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: Available: the economics of messy code and the Boy Scout Rule. Not available as a chapter: Meaningful Names, Unit Tests or Concurrency. Their titles/index references do not substitute for their missing contents. Start with one short lesson rather than treating every reference page as a daily assignment.

children.title: Publication material and navigating the book

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Use publication details, contents, bibliography and the index without mistaking navigation for missing teaching.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 1–18, 27–30, 45–67. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Credits and provenance
slides.body:
Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship is credited to Robert C. Martin and the Object Mentors. The title page names Michael C. Feathers, Timothy R. Ottinger, Jeffrey J. Langr, Brett L. Schuchert, James W. Grenning and Kevin Dean Wampler. The excerpt’s copyright page states © 2009 Pearson Education, Inc.; this printing is identified as January 2015.

The dedication, publisher contacts, ISBNs and series titles remain in the source reference. Acknowledgments credit artists Jeniffer Kohnke and Angela Brooks, reviewers, publishers, Object Mentors and other colleagues.

slides.title: The contents are a roadmap
slides.body:
The contents list the complete book’s chapters: Clean Code, Meaningful Names, Functions, Comments, Formatting, Objects and Data Structures, Error Handling, Boundaries, Unit Tests, Classes, Systems, Emergence, Concurrency, Successive Refinement, JUnit Internals, Refactoring SerialDate, and Smells and Heuristics, followed by the concurrency appendix and index.

Only Chapter 1 is present as chapter text in this upload. Use the contents to plan later reading; do not infer full rules from headings alone.

slides.title: Printed pages versus PDF pages
slides.body:
PDF page 31 is printed page 1. Roman-numbered front matter comes before it. The index starts at PDF page 47, printed page 413. An index reference such as 120 points to printed page 120 of the full book, not PDF page 120 or a page present in this excerpt.

The source reference labels the PDF page explicitly and retains printed numbers. Chapter 1’s bibliography names Kent Beck’s Implementation Patterns (2007) and Donald E. Knuth’s Literate Programming (1992).

slides.title: The cover essay
slides.body:
On the Cover identifies the cover subject as M104, the Sombrero Galaxy, and describes a visible-light Hubble and infrared Spitzer composite. It also contains the author’s imaginative comparison with science-fiction explosions and speculation about a central black hole. Treat that speculation as the author’s narrative, not as established astrophysical explanation.

The supplied course theme image is a separate color reference; it is not evidence for the cover essay. The essay, image credit and publisher registration offer and final Safari Books Online advertisement are preserved as source material.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: An index says a topic appears on printed page 120. Can you open it in this 67-page course source? Explain the page-number distinction.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: No. The source jumps from Chapter 1 to the full book’s index; printed page 120 is not included. PDF page numbers locate available pages, while the index points into the full book. Use the relevant source page to inspect the entry, then obtain the missing chapter before claiming its detailed guidance.

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Explain why everyday code care contributes to software quality alongside architecture.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 19–23. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Small work supports large work
slides.body:
Coplien uses architecture and a licorice-box proverb to argue that small details matter. A well-planned building can still be undermined by a door that does not close; a well-planned system can still be undermined by careless names, layout and local decisions.

Planning and architecture remain useful. Attention to local construction gives a team the proficiency and trust needed for larger work.

slides.title: Production is only one part of the lifecycle
slides.body:
The foreword contrasts fast production with ongoing maintenance. Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) supplies a metaphor: do not wait for equipment to fail before caring for it. Inspect, prevent deterioration, and design for maintainability.

Coplien’s statement that maintenance accounts for 80% or more of software work is a historical claim in this foreword, not a measured statistic about your current team.

slides.title: Preventive work and replacement
slides.body:
The maintenance analogy progresses from fixing failures to preventive inspection, making new systems maintainable, and eventually replacing obsolete equipment. In code, local refactoring can prevent a small problem from spreading.

The foreword also discusses replacement and a Brooks time interval; these are contextual arguments, not an instruction to rewrite a production application on a fixed calendar. Chapter 1 later explains the costs of an uncontrolled grand redesign.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Pick a small module you understand. Identify one detail that slows a reader and one larger structural concern. Which can you safely improve today?

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: A vague variable name can be renamed with its references and checked immediately. A database boundary may require broader evidence and planning. Caring about the small issue supports larger design work; it does not prove that the architecture is already correct.

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Translate the foreword’s 5S maintenance metaphor into concrete code habits.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 20–21. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Organization and tidiness
slides.body:
**Seiri — organization/sort:** know where things are; choose names that reveal meaning.

**Seiton — tidiness/systematize:** keep a thing where readers expect to find it. If responsibility has wandered, consider refactoring it into the appropriate module.

A reader should not have to search unrelated files for one concept.

slides.title: Cleaning and standardization
slides.body:
**Seiso — cleaning/shine:** remove waste. The foreword specifically criticizes commented-out lines that preserve history or wishes. Version control is an appropriate place for history; active source should communicate current behavior.

**Seiketsu — standardization:** agree as a team on consistent style and practices. A shared convention reduces avoidable surprises; agreement is more useful than each person imposing a private preference.

slides.title: Self-discipline
slides.body:
**Shutsuke — self-discipline**, using the spelling in the supplied text: follow practices, reflect frequently and be willing to change.

A cleanup that happens once is not a maintenance habit. Make small reviews repeatable. These are analogies from maintenance, not an automated scoring formula for code quality.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Classify these improvements using the five disciplines: clarify a name, move validation beside related validation, remove dead commented code, adopt a shared formatter, and review before every commit.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: Clarify a name: Seiri. Move related validation: Seiton. Remove dead commented code: Seiso. Agree on formatting: Seiketsu. Repeat the review habit and reflect on it: Shutsuke. The categories overlap; use them to guide care, not to argue about labels.

children.title: Design as ongoing repair and honest quality

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Connect refactoring, concrete design and an honest definition of done.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 21–23. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Design continues after release
slides.body:
Coplien invokes Christopher Alexander’s local acts of repair and the continual rework of poetry. Design is a process rather than a finished drawing. Maintenance does not automatically mean failure; refining the design can add value.

His contrast is between wasteful manufacturing rework and valuable design refinement. The architectural relationship of coupling and cohesion becomes concrete in actual code.

slides.title: Consistency is useful evidence, not proof
slides.body:
The foreword recounts informal Bell Labs findings linking consistent indentation with lower bug density. Preserve the distinction: this is a reported historical observation, not proof that a formatter guarantees correctness or that indentation alone causes fewer bugs.

Look at what the code does, how responsibilities fit together and whether a change can be safely checked.

slides.title: Be honest about the state of the code
slides.body:
The closing argument is honesty with yourself and colleagues. Make unfinished work visible; include refactoring in what your team means by Done when appropriate. Neither architecture nor clean code requires perfection.

A useful report describes the issue, its consequence, the evidence and the remaining uncertainty. Quietly hiding a known shortcut makes the next person’s decisions harder.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Write a two-sentence status for code that passes the happy path but has no check for an empty input. Include the remaining work.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: “The normal input is covered and passes. Empty input behavior is not yet specified or tested; I will agree on that behavior and add a focused test before calling the change done.” This is more honest and useful than “Everything works.”

questions.prompt: Which action best demonstrates Seiton?
options: Make every name shorter
Place validation with the module responsible for it
Delay all cleanup until a rewrite
questions.explanation: Seiton concerns expected location and organization of work; names alone are Seiri’s emphasis.

questions.prompt: What does the indentation anecdote establish?
options: Formatting guarantees correctness
All architectural decisions are irrelevant
The foreword reports an association; tests and design review still matter
questions.explanation: An informal historical association does not prove causation or replace checking actual behavior.

questions.prompt: Which status best reflects honesty about quality?
options: Works on my example, so it is finished
Normal input passes; failure handling still needs verification
Do not mention incomplete checks
questions.explanation: State what is known and what remains, so the team can make informed decisions.

questions.prompt: Which habit matches self-discipline?
options: Reviewing and refining work regularly
Applying standards only on release day
Choosing a different convention for each function
questions.explanation: The foreword emphasizes sustained practices, reflection and willingness to change.

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Distinguish knowing a principle from being able to apply it to real code.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 25–28. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Two ingredients
slides.body:
The introduction says craftsmanship requires knowledge and work. Learning principles, patterns, practices and heuristics is necessary; applying them repeatedly is also necessary. Knowing the equations of a bicycle does not mean you can ride it.

Code learning needs the equivalent of riding: read code, try a change, see what goes wrong, and revise your decision.

slides.title: Watch the decisions, not just the result
slides.body:
The author asks readers to observe successes, failures, reversals and the costs of bad choices. Read code closely enough to explain what is right and what is wrong. Follow how modules are taken apart and rebuilt.

For this excerpt, the original later case studies are unavailable. The course’s small JavaScript clinic is authored practice, not a replacement or reconstruction of those missing chapters.

slides.title: Make the work observable
slides.body:
Record the behavior before a change, the improvement you intend, the transformation, and the check afterward. If you cannot explain why the change is better, write down that gap and investigate.

A useful five-minute exercise can be one function, one safe rename, or one explanation of a confusing branch. Completing slides is not evidence that you can refactor a real system.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Explain a function in your own words without editing it. Then predict the output for one normal case and one edge case, and check both in your environment.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: A good explanation names the inputs, output, assumptions and side effects. If a prediction fails, revise your mental model before refactoring. You are practicing understanding and feedback, rather than memorizing a slogan.

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Explain how the complete book connects general guidance with specific refactoring decisions.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 26–27. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: The book’s three parts
slides.body:
The introduction describes principles and practices first, detailed case studies second, and a collection of smells and heuristics third. The case studies grow in complexity and connect narrative decisions to code listings.

This upload gives the description of that structure, not the case-study chapters or the final heuristics chapter itself.

slides.title: A heuristic needs context
slides.body:
Forward references such as [H22] connect a particular change to a heuristic. A cross-reference at the end of the full book points back to every occurrence. The valuable knowledge is the relationship between the rule and the decision that prompted it.

A rule without its trigger, assumptions and tradeoff can become a reflex applied in the wrong place.

slides.title: Turn a guideline into a decision record
slides.body:
Use four questions: What problem did I observe? Which transformation addresses it? What behavior must stay unchanged? How will I verify that?

Keep the guideline as a reason to investigate. Do not invent the text of a numbered book heuristic from an isolated reference or index entry.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Take “reduce duplication.” Write a case where sharing logic helps and a case where combining two similar-looking functions would be premature.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: Sharing a genuinely identical permission rule can prevent updates from diverging. Combining two rules that only look similar but have different domain reasons can create a misleading abstraction. Explain the shared idea and expected change pattern before extracting it. This tradeoff discussion is authored guidance, not a quotation from an unavailable heuristic.

questions.prompt: Why does the introduction compare coding with bicycle riding?
options: Reading equations is enough to master a skill
Knowledge must be paired with hands-on practice
Programming principles have no value
questions.explanation: Principles matter, but repeated practice develops the ability to apply them.

questions.prompt: What makes a case-study heuristic useful?
options: Its relationship to a concrete decision and its context
Its short label alone
The assumption that it works everywhere
questions.explanation: The introduction stresses seeing why a particular transformation was made.

questions.prompt: What does an index reference to a missing chapter provide?
options: That chapter’s full content
An executable example
A pointer into the full book, not the missing explanation
questions.explanation: The index is retained completely, but absent chapters are not reconstructed as source text.

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Explain why tools and higher abstractions do not remove the need for precise requirements.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 31–32. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Code expresses the details
slides.body:
Chapter 1 argues that executable specifications must be detailed, formal and accurate enough for a machine. Higher-level languages and domain-specific languages can raise abstraction, but cannot eliminate required precision.

The author’s prediction about the future is his position in this historical text. The practical lesson is to resolve ambiguous behavior instead of assuming a tool will infer every unstated need.

slides.title: A vague requirement hides choices
Specify before generating or implementing
slides.body:
Write examples of accepted inputs and expected results, including edge cases. Those examples can become executable checks. A code generator or coding assistant still produces an implementation of a contract that someone must understand and review.

The source’s argument is about necessary precision, not proof that any particular modern tool succeeds or fails.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Specify getCompletedLessons for an empty array, completed false, missing completed, and completed "true". Should the function mutate the input?

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: For the contract shown: empty input returns []; false, missing and the string "true" are excluded; only boolean true is included. filter returns a new array and does not mutate the input array. Invalid non-array input is outside this example’s stated contract and needs a separate decision.

children.title: Bad code and the total cost of owning a mess

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Trace how a convenient shortcut can turn into long-term difficulty changing a system.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 33–34. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: The product story
slides.body:
Martin recounts a popular product whose rushed implementation accumulated problems. Releases slowed, bugs persisted, load times grew and crashes increased. An employee later attributed the failure to an unmanageable codebase.

This is an anecdote in the source, not a controlled study or a claim that every business failure has the same cause.

slides.title: Wading and postponed cleanup
slides.body:
Wading describes trying to understand tangled code before a change. Deadline pressure, fatigue and a long backlog can encourage a working mess. The chapter names LeBlanc’s law: postponing cleanup indefinitely often means it never happens.

A better decision names the specific debt, its consequence and the time or trigger for addressing it. An unspecified “later” is not a maintenance plan.

slides.title: The feedback loop
slides.body:
As tangles grow, a small change can break unrelated parts. More effort goes into understanding the mess. Management may add staff, but newcomers do not yet understand the design and feel the same pressure to ship. Their changes can add more disorder.

Figure 1-1 illustrates productivity declining toward zero. It is a conceptual figure, not a dataset from which this course can calculate a numeric productivity forecast.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Describe a shortcut in an app you know. Map it through this chain: confusion → slower change → pressure → further shortcut. Give one intervention.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: Example: duplicated completion rules diverge, so updates require searching several files; a deadline encourages copying a fourth rule. An intervention is to agree on one explicit rule, test it, and route callers through it. The improvement must address observed behavior, not just reduce a line count.

children.title: The grand redesign and professional responsibility

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Explain rewrite risk and communicate code-quality consequences under deadline pressure.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 35–36. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: The replacement race
slides.body:
The “grand redesign” story splits a team into a new implementation group and maintainers of the old system. The replacement must match existing behavior while keeping up with ongoing changes. The finish line moves.

Martin describes long projects in which a replacement becomes messy before it ships. The argument favors sustained care; it does not prove that every rewrite is wrong.

slides.title: Attitude and responsibility
slides.body:
The chapter criticizes blaming requirements, schedules or management while hiding technical consequences. Programmers participate in validating requirements, estimates and design choices. They should provide honest technical information and defend necessary engineering work.

The doctor/hand-washing analogy emphasizes explaining risks when the person requesting speed lacks that expertise. It is an analogy, not a software regulation.

slides.title: The primal conundrum
slides.body:
Developers know previous messes slow them down yet feel pressure to create new messes to meet deadlines. Martin’s answer is that keeping code clean is part of going fast.

In a real discussion, identify the smallest safe deliverable, preserve necessary checks, and explain the cost of deferred work. Do not turn the author’s emphatic position into an unsupported guarantee that every cleanup immediately saves time.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: A manager requests two new features today. One touches a confusing permission rule. Write a response that includes a smaller scope and the necessary check.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: “I can finish the display change today. The permission change affects access decisions, so I need to clarify the rule and test allowed and denied cases before releasing it. We can ship the display work first and schedule the permission change with those checks.” This supplies consequences and options instead of quietly skipping care.

questions.prompt: A generator creates code from a vague request. What responsibility remains?
options: Assume every edge case was inferred correctly
Define the missing behavior and check the implementation
Treat compilation as proof of business correctness
questions.explanation: Executable behavior still requires precise requirements and verification.

questions.prompt: Why can adding developers to a tangled project fail to restore speed?
options: Developers never improve systems
A larger team automatically duplicates all features
Newcomers lack design context and can add more tangles under pressure
questions.explanation: The source describes a feedback loop of low context, pressure and worsening change cost.

questions.prompt: What is the moving target in a grand redesign?
options: The replacement must match the old system while that system keeps changing
The old system stops receiving updates automatically
A new codebase cannot develop technical debt
questions.explanation: Feature parity and continued changes create an ongoing race.

questions.prompt: What is the professional response to risky deadline pressure?
options: Hide shortcuts to protect the schedule
State consequences and offer a smaller safe scope
Promise that every rewrite takes less time
questions.explanation: Provide honest engineering information and defend the work needed for a safe change.

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Distinguish noticing messy code from knowing how to improve it without changing its behavior.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 36–37. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Recognition is not execution
slides.body:
The Art of Clean Code compares judging a painting with being able to paint. Seeing that a module is confusing does not tell you how to transform it. Code sense includes seeing alternative designs and choosing a workable sequence.

The skill is developed through small techniques and repeated decisions, not only through a vocabulary of smells.

slides.title: Refactoring preserves the contract
slides.body:
A behavior-preserving transformation changes internal structure while keeping the observable contract. A rename, extraction or movement can be a refactoring if callers still receive the same results and side effects.

Changing eligibility, throwing a new error or reordering an externally meaningful sequence is a behavior change and needs its own decision. Label it honestly.

slides.title: Plan a small sequence
slides.body:
First understand the behavior. Add checks around what matters. Make one understandable transformation. Run the checks and inspect the difference. Repeat only when the next change has a clear purpose.

This is authored practice that makes the source’s transformation idea concrete. It is not a full reconstruction of a missing case study.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: You rename a function and also change its result from undefined to null. Is the whole change behavior-preserving? Explain.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: No. The rename may preserve behavior if references are updated, but changing the result can affect callers. Separate the contract change, specify its effects and verify them. Passing one happy-path test is not evidence that every caller is unaffected.

children.title: Stroustrup and Booch: focus and clarity

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Compare efficiency, focus, clear control flow and direct expression of intent.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 37–39. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Bjarne Stroustrup’s emphasis
slides.body:
Stroustrup values elegant and efficient code with straightforward logic, minimal dependencies, a clear error strategy and strong performance. He emphasizes doing one thing well.

Martin interprets this as attention to details including errors, resource leaks, race conditions and inconsistent naming. Wasteful execution can tempt unprincipled optimization; muddy purpose can hide bugs.

slides.title: The broken-windows connection
slides.body:
Martin connects neglected code with the broken-windows metaphor from Dave Thomas and Andy Hunt: visible disorder can encourage the next person to accept more disorder.

The metaphor describes a possible maintenance habit. It is not evidence that a single ugly line inevitably destroys a project. A small, justified improvement can change what the next reader expects.

slides.title: Grady Booch’s emphasis
slides.body:
Booch values simple, direct code that reads clearly, exposes the designer’s intent, and uses crisp abstractions and straightforward control flow. Martin interprets crispness as decisive and free from unnecessary detail.

Readable code lets a reader follow the problem and see why the solution fits. Speculative structure that serves no current need can obscure that story.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Review one function for purpose, dependencies, error handling and reader effort. Name one improvement that helps both focus and clarity.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: Example: move unrelated reporting out of a calculation while retaining the same reporting behavior at its caller. The calculation becomes easier to explain and test. Verify the ordering and side effects; do not call the change safe merely because the extracted function is shorter.

children.title: Thomas and Feathers: changeability and care

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Explain why readable code also needs checks, clear dependencies and deliberate care.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 39–40. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Dave Thomas’s definition
slides.body:
Dave Thomas emphasizes code another developer can read and enhance. He names unit and acceptance tests, meaningful names, one clear way to do a task, explicit minimal dependencies, and a minimal API.

Readable and changeable are related but different: understanding a function does not by itself show that a change will be safe.

slides.title: Tests and literate communication
slides.body:
Martin strongly endorses tests as part of clean code. Thomas’s literate-code point recognizes that language constructs alone may not express every necessary piece of information.

Preserve useful contracts or rationale where needed. This excerpt does not supply the later Comments or Unit Tests chapters, so do not claim their detailed rules are included here.

slides.title: Michael Feathers’s definition
slides.body:
Feathers emphasizes the visible care of the author: the code appears thought through, simple and orderly, with details attended to. Martin summarizes this as caring for code.

Care is not decoration. A neat-looking function with a hidden failure path still needs work. Look for evidence that responsibilities, constraints and likely changes have been considered.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: A function has excellent names but no tests and reads a global variable silently. Explain two remaining change risks.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: The result depends on hidden state, so callers and tests cannot see the whole contract. Missing tests make it harder to detect a regression. Make the dependency explicit where appropriate and add focused checks before changing it. Naming is valuable but does not establish changeability by itself.

children.title: Jeffries: simple design and small abstractions

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Apply the priorities of simple code and explain the idea behind an abstraction.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 40–41. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: The priority order
slides.body:
Jeffries presents Beck’s simple-code rules in order: run all tests; remove duplication; express the system’s design ideas; minimize entities such as classes and methods.

Do not remove an entity in a way that breaks behavior or hides the design just to win a size metric. The order matters.

slides.title: Duplication reveals a missing idea
slides.body:
Repeated behavior may mean an idea has not been represented clearly. Jeffries revisits names, asks whether an object or method does more than one thing, and uses extraction to express intent.

Expressiveness extends beyond names: boundaries and responsibilities should make the system’s ideas visible. Similar syntax alone does not prove that two policies are the same idea.

slides.title: Finding things in a collection
Practice
slides.body: Write the contract for findLessonById. Explain why creating a configurable repository framework for every imaginable query would not follow the small-abstraction example.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: The example returns the first matching lesson or undefined and does not reorder or mutate the list. A large generic framework introduces dependencies and choices beyond the current need. Preserve the lookup contract and add broader capabilities only when there is a concrete requirement. If duplicate IDs are possible, specify whether first-match behavior is acceptable.

children.title: Cunningham: unsurprising code and domain language

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Explain how naming and boundaries can make the next step in a program predictable.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 41–42. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: A reader’s expectations
slides.body:
Cunningham’s test is whether routines turn out as a reader expects. Martin contrasts that with puzzling modules that require the reader to reconstruct tangled reasoning. Clean modules set up the next module clearly.

Expectation is a contract: a lookup should not unexpectedly save data, and a name about completion should not silently mean mere visitation.

slides.title: Make the language fit the problem
slides.body:
Cunningham describes beauty when a program makes its language seem designed for the problem. Domain names and small abstractions can let code speak in terms of lessons, enrollments and completion instead of unrelated storage details.

Martin puts responsibility on the programmer rather than on a favored language. No language automatically makes the design understandable.

slides.title: Use surprise as a review prompt
slides.body:
Before reading a routine, predict its inputs, result and effects from its name and call site. Then compare the prediction with the implementation.

A mismatch is a reason to inspect the naming or boundary. It is not automatically a bug: a documented contract may intentionally differ from your first assumption.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: A function named findLesson both returns a lesson and sends an analytics event. What question should a reviewer ask?

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: “Is the analytics side effect part of the intended and documented lookup contract?” If it is not, consider making the effect explicit at the caller or giving the routine a name that communicates it. Verify behavior before moving it, including whether the event should occur on a failed lookup.

questions.prompt: Which concern is central to Stroustrup’s definition?
options: Straightforward logic, efficiency and a complete error strategy
The largest possible framework
Only visual formatting
questions.explanation: His perspective combines elegance, focus, dependencies, errors and efficiency.

questions.prompt: What does Dave Thomas add beyond ease of reading?
options: More hidden dependencies
Ease of enhancement supported by tests and explicit boundaries
An API for every possible future feature
questions.explanation: Changeability, tests, minimal dependencies and a clear API are part of his definition.

questions.prompt: What is the first priority in Jeffries’s simple-code list?
options: Minimize the number of functions at any cost
Remove every repeated word
Run all the tests
questions.explanation: The stated priority order begins with tests, then duplication, expression and entity count.

questions.prompt: Which routine best fits Cunningham’s expectation criterion?
options: A lookup that secretly changes permissions
A named lookup that follows its explicit result and side-effect contract
A function whose name has no relation to its behavior
questions.explanation: A reader should be able to predict the routine from its intent and context.

questions.prompt: What does code sense add to spotting a mess?
options: A sequence of behavior-preserving improvements
A universal maximum line count
Permission to skip checking results
questions.explanation: It includes seeing alternatives and choosing transformations, not just recognizing disorder.

children.title: Schools of thought and professional judgment

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Use the book’s strong recommendations as a school of practice while evaluating context.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 42–43. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: The Object Mentor school
slides.body:
Martin explicitly presents the book as the Object Mentor School of Clean Code. Its authors state opinions strongly because they have practiced them over decades. He uses martial-arts schools as an analogy for learning a coherent approach.

Practice one approach carefully enough to understand it. Later, broaden your understanding with other approaches.

slides.title: Strong guidance is not final authority
slides.body:
The text also says other schools can be professional and that some recommendations are controversial. Disagreement can coexist with respect for the reasoning and experience behind a practice.

Evaluate a recommendation against behavior, readers, change cost and evidence. Avoid treating every aesthetic preference as an absolute correctness rule.

slides.title: Separate principle from local convention
slides.body:
A principle such as communicating intent can support several naming conventions. Team consistency and a demonstrated reader benefit can matter more than adopting the author’s exact spelling choices.

In a review, state the problem and consequence before proposing a convention. “I prefer it” is different from “this name leads callers to expect the wrong result.”

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Two teammates disagree about a helper extraction. Write one question that tests whether the extraction is useful rather than asking who follows the right school.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: “Can a reader now identify the responsibility and safely change it with less surrounding context?” Also check whether the helper hides important behavior or creates indirection without a benefit. Use a concrete call site and test, not a slogan.

children.title: We are authors and code is read repeatedly

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Explain why improving reader comprehension can help future changes.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 43–44. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Programmers have readers
slides.body:
The chapter compares a programmer with an author responsible for communication. Readers include teammates and your future self. A line of code contributes to a larger explanation of the problem and solution.

Names, structure, contracts and direct control flow should help that reader reconstruct the intent.

slides.title: The edit-session observation
slides.body:
Martin describes replaying edit sessions in which much of the time was spent scrolling, inspecting initialization, checking callers and examining subclasses. He argues that reading greatly exceeds writing and gives a ratio above 10:1.

Treat that ratio as the author’s observation and argument, not a measured ratio for every developer. The supported practical point is that writing a change requires understanding surrounding code.

slides.title: Reduce the cost of understanding
slides.body:
Ask what the reader must discover before editing: where data comes from, which callers depend on it, what a flag means and whether an effect happens. Make necessary information easy to find.

A shorter function is not automatically easier to read if it scatters one coherent idea across many poorly named helpers. Evaluate reader effort in context.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Describe one time you had to inspect several files before making a small change. What information would have reduced that search?

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: A clear contract, explicit dependency, meaningful name or focused test could answer the question locally. For example, a test stating that a missing lesson returns undefined removes guesswork. Record the actual missing information before rearranging code.

children.title: The Boy Scout Rule and continuous improvement

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Choose a small cleanup that leaves the code easier to maintain.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 44. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Keep the code clean over time
slides.body:
The Boy Scout Rule applies the campground principle to code: leave it a little better than you found it. Writing clean code once is insufficient if later changes let it decay.

The source names improved variable names, breaking a large function, removing small duplication and simplifying a composite condition as possible small cleanups.

slides.title: Make a bounded improvement
slides.body:
Choose a change related to the work you understand. Describe the expected benefit, keep the difference reviewable and verify behavior. Continuous care does not require a whole-system rewrite during every bug fix.

An authored example replaces an unexplained flag name with isCompleted while preserving its boolean meaning and updating its references.

slides.title: Review the consequence
slides.body:
Ask: Did I clarify a real ambiguity? Did I preserve behavior? Did I introduce a new dependency? Can the next person understand the improvement?

If cleanup needs a contract change, separate and explain it. The rule is an attitude of maintenance, not permission to hide unrelated work in a small commit.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Choose exactly one cleanup in a function you understand. Write a before/after reason and the check you will run.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: “Rename d to completedAt because the value is a completion timestamp, not a duration. Update all references and run the completion tests.” The reason communicates the value’s meaning; the check helps show that the rename preserved behavior.

children.title: Principles, bibliography and the limits of reading

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Recognize the chapter’s follow-up references and why practice remains necessary.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 45. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Prequel and principles
slides.body:
Martin describes Clean Code as a prequel to his 2002 Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices (PPP). He names the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP), Open Closed Principle (OCP) and Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP), and says PPP describes them in depth.

This excerpt does not give their full explanations. A reference to a principle is not the same as a complete lesson on it.

slides.title: What a book can provide
slides.body:
The conclusion compares a programming book to a book about art. It can expose tools, thought processes, good and bad examples and transformations. It cannot promise to make a reader skilled or automatically provide code sense.

The reader must practice, inspect outcomes and revise decisions.

slides.title: Use references honestly
slides.body:
The chapter bibliography points to Implementation Patterns by Kent Beck and Literate Programming by Donald E. Knuth. The full index points into missing parts of the book as well as available pages.

Preserve the references so you can follow up. Do not claim that this course includes the entire contents of those other works.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Write a follow-up learning plan containing one available concept, one code exercise and one genuinely missing chapter or principle reference.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: Available concept: reader expectations. Exercise: make one lookup’s contract explicit and test not-found behavior. Missing follow-up: read the actual Unit Tests chapter or PPP’s principle explanations. This distinguishes learning from the supplied material from obtaining additional sources.

questions.prompt: How does Martin describe his school of thought?
options: The only professional approach with final authority
A practiced approach that can be learned alongside other schools
A set of rules that cannot be questioned
questions.explanation: The chapter acknowledges controversy and other professional schools.

questions.prompt: What supports making code easy to read?
options: A change requires understanding surrounding code
Readers only inspect formatting
Generated code has no readers
questions.explanation: The edit-session argument links reader comprehension to effective modification.

questions.prompt: Which change best illustrates a bounded Boy Scout cleanup?
options: Rewrite the entire application without a plan
Hide an eligibility change inside a rename
Clarify one misleading name and verify its references
questions.explanation: A small, justified, behavior-preserving improvement is enough.

questions.prompt: What is actually present about SRP, OCP and DIP?
options: Full chapters and implementations
Their names and a follow-up reference to PPP
A formal proof for each principle
questions.explanation: The excerpt mentions the principles but directs deeper study to another book.

children.title: Refactor a lesson lookup without changing its contract

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Practice naming, one responsibility, simple abstraction and verification in an original JavaScript example.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 37, 40–44. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Establish behavior first
Name the idea
Check meaningful cases
Consider the next improvement
slides.body:
With the contract established, Array.find may make the search idea more direct. Check the same cases before accepting the change. A Map implementation can change duplicate-ID behavior unless you deliberately preserve first-match semantics.

One abstraction permits a later implementation change; it does not make that change automatically safe.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Replace the loop with Array.find. Run the checks, then explain why a Map constructed from all records can return the wrong duplicate.

slides.title: Worked self-check

children.title: Capstone review and your next small change

slides.title: Learning objective
slides.body:
Combine the source’s perspectives into an evidence-based review of a small module.

Source: supplied Clean Code excerpt, PDF pages 19–45. The following explanations and exercises are authored study material; the complete extracted source appears in module 08.

slides.title: Build a review in five questions
slides.body:
1. **Intent:** Can a reader predict this routine?
2. **Behavior:** Are normal, missing and failure cases explicit and checked?
3. **Focus:** Is one responsibility obscured by unrelated effects?
4. **Changeability:** Are dependencies and shared ideas clear?
5. **Care:** What one justified improvement can I leave behind?

This checklist is an authored synthesis of the excerpt, not the missing Smells and Heuristics chapter.

slides.title: Make a claim with evidence
slides.body:
Weak review: “This is bad code.”

Useful review: “The function is named findLesson, but it also updates completion. A caller cannot predict that side effect from the name. Please make the update explicit and verify both successful and missing lookups.”

State the concrete trigger, consequence and proposed check. Do not require an extraction only because a line count is high.

slides.title: Record the change
slides.body:
Write a short before/after note: original behavior, reader difficulty, chosen transformation, checks passed, remaining uncertainty.

A passing module quiz shows recall and judgment in these scenarios. Only working on real code provides evidence about your ability to make a safe change.

slides.title: Practice
slides.body: Select a real helper from one of your projects. Explain it without looking at the implementation, compare that explanation with the code, and make one behavior-preserving improvement. Keep the diff and your checks.

slides.title: Worked self-check
slides.body: The submission is your explanation, a bounded diff and check results. A valid outcome may be “No change needed; the routine already matches its contract.” If a behavior change is necessary, identify it separately. The goal is deliberate judgment and care, not the greatest number of edits.

questions.prompt: The original lookup returns the first duplicate ID. Which replacement preserves that contract?
options: Array.find with the same equality check
A Map that overwrites earlier duplicate keys
Always return the last matching record
questions.explanation: Array.find retains first-match behavior. The other choices select a later value.

questions.prompt: Which check addresses a meaningful lookup boundary?
options: Only check whether the function name is short
Verify that a missing ID returns undefined
Only count the number of lines
questions.explanation: Not-found behavior is part of the explicit contract and can regress during refactoring.

questions.prompt: Which review comment is most useful?
options: This feels wrong
All functions must have three lines
This lookup changes completion unexpectedly; make the effect explicit and test it
questions.explanation: A concrete mismatch, its consequence and a verification request support a reviewable decision.

```text
                                                       Foreword

One of our favorite candies here in Denmark is Ga-Jol, whose strong licorice vapors are a
perfect complement to our damp and often chilly weather. Part of the charm of Ga-Jol to
us Danes is the wise or witty sayings printed on the flap of every box top. I bought a two-
pack of the delicacy this morning and found that it bore this old Danish saw:
     Ærlighed i små ting er ikke nogen lille ting.
“Honesty in small things is not a small thing.” It was a good omen consistent with what I
already wanted to say here. Small things matter. This is a book about humble concerns
whose value is nonetheless far from small.
     God is in the details, said the architect Ludwig mies van der Rohe. This quote recalls
contemporary arguments about the role of architecture in software development, and par-
ticularly in the Agile world. Bob and I occasionally find ourselves passionately engaged in
this dialogue. And yes, mies van der Rohe was attentive to utility and to the timeless forms
of building that underlie great architecture. On the other hand, he also personally selected
every doorknob for every house he designed. Why? Because small things matter.
     In our ongoing “debate” on TDD, Bob and I have discovered that we agree that soft-
ware architecture has an important place in development, though we likely have different
visions of exactly what that means. Such quibbles are relatively unimportant, however,
because we can accept for granted that responsible professionals give some time to think-
ing and planning at the outset of a project. The late-1990s notions of design driven only by
the tests and the code are long gone. Yet attentiveness to detail is an even more critical
foundation of professionalism than is any grand vision. First, it is through practice in the
small that professionals gain proficiency and trust for practice in the large. Second, the
smallest bit of sloppy construction, of the door that does not close tightly or the slightly
crooked tile on the floor, or even the messy desk, completely dispels the charm of the
larger whole. That is what clean code is about.
     Still, architecture is just one metaphor for software development, and in particular for
that part of software that delivers the initial product in the same sense that an architect
delivers a pristine building. In these days of Scrum and Agile, the focus is on quickly
bringing product to market. We want the factory running at top speed to produce software.
These are human factories: thinking, feeling coders who are working from a product back-
log or user story to create product. The manufacturing metaphor looms ever strong in such
thinking. The production aspects of Japanese auto manufacturing, of an assembly-line
world, inspire much of Scrum.

                                                                                         xix
```

```text
xx                                                                                 Foreword


     Yet even in the auto industry, the bulk of the work lies not in manufacturing but in
maintenance—or its avoidance. In software, 80% or more of what we do is quaintly called
“maintenance”: the act of repair. Rather than embracing the typical Western focus on pro-
ducing good software, we should be thinking more like home repairmen in the building
industry, or auto mechanics in the automotive field. What does Japanese management have
to say about that?
     In about 1951, a quality approach called Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) came
on the Japanese scene. Its focus is on maintenance rather than on production. One of the
major pillars of TPM is the set of so-called 5S principles. 5S is a set of disciplines—and
here I use the term “discipline” instructively. These 5S principles are in fact at the founda-
tions of Lean—another buzzword on the Western scene, and an increasingly prominent
buzzword in software circles. These principles are not an option. As Uncle Bob relates in
his front matter, good software practice requires such discipline: focus, presence of mind,
and thinking. It is not always just about doing, about pushing the factory equipment to pro-
duce at the optimal velocity. The 5S philosophy comprises these concepts:
 • Seiri, or organization (think “sort” in English). Knowing where things are—using
   approaches such as suitable naming—is crucial. You think naming identifiers isn’t
   important? Read on in the following chapters.
 • Seiton, or tidiness (think “systematize” in English). There is an old American saying:
   A place for everything, and everything in its place. A piece of code should be where
   you expect to find it—and, if not, you should re-factor to get it there.
 • Seiso, or cleaning (think “shine” in English): Keep the workplace free of hanging
   wires, grease, scraps, and waste. What do the authors here say about littering your
   code with comments and commented-out code lines that capture history or wishes for
   the future? Get rid of them.
 • Seiketsu, or standardization: The group agrees about how to keep the workplace clean.
   Do you think this book says anything about having a consistent coding style and set of
   practices within the group? Where do those standards come from? Read on.
 • Shutsuke, or discipline (self-discipline). This means having the discipline to follow the
   practices and to frequently reflect on one’s work and be willing to change.
     If you take up the challenge—yes, the challenge—of reading and applying this book,
you’ll come to understand and appreciate the last point. Here, we are finally driving to the
roots of responsible professionalism in a profession that should be concerned with the life
cycle of a product. As we maintain automobiles and other machines under TPM, break-
down maintenance—waiting for bugs to surface—is the exception. Instead, we go up a
level: inspect the machines every day and fix wearing parts before they break, or do the
equivalent of the proverbial 10,000-mile oil change to forestall wear and tear. In code,
refactor mercilessly. You can improve yet one level further, as the TPM movement inno-
vated over 50 years ago: build machines that are more maintainable in the first place. Mak-
ing your code readable is as important as making it executable. The ultimate practice,
introduced in TPM circles around 1960, is to focus on introducing entire new machines or
```

slides.body:
```text
Foreword                                                                                   xxi


replacing old ones. As Fred Brooks admonishes us, we should probably re-do major soft-
ware chunks from scratch every seven years or so to sweep away creeping cruft. Perhaps
we should update Brooks’ time constant to an order of weeks, days or hours instead of
years. That’s where detail lies.
      There is great power in detail, yet there is something humble and profound about this
approach to life, as we might stereotypically expect from any approach that claims Japa-
nese roots. But this is not only an Eastern outlook on life; English and American folk wis-
dom are full of such admonishments. The Seiton quote from above flowed from the pen of
an Ohio minister who literally viewed neatness “as a remedy for every degree of evil.”
How about Seiso? Cleanliness is next to godliness. As beautiful as a house is, a messy
desk robs it of its splendor. How about Shutsuke in these small matters? He who is faithful
in little is faithful in much. How about being eager to re-factor at the responsible time,
strengthening one’s position for subsequent “big” decisions, rather than putting it off? A
stitch in time saves nine. The early bird catches the worm. Don’t put off until tomorrow
what you can do today. (Such was the original sense of the phrase “the last responsible
moment” in Lean until it fell into the hands of software consultants.) How about calibrat-
ing the place of small, individual efforts in a grand whole? Mighty oaks from little acorns
grow. Or how about integrating simple preventive work into everyday life? An ounce of
prevention is worth a pound of cure. An apple a day keeps the doctor away. Clean code
honors the deep roots of wisdom beneath our broader culture, or our culture as it once was,
or should be, and can be with attentiveness to detail.
      Even in the grand architectural literature we find saws that hark back to these sup-
posed details. Think of mies van der Rohe’s doorknobs. That’s seiri. That’s being attentive
to every variable name. You should name a variable using the same care with which you
name a first-born child.
      As every homeowner knows, such care and ongoing refinement never come to an end.
The architect Christopher Alexander—father of patterns and pattern languages—views
every act of design itself as a small, local act of repair. And he views the craftsmanship of
fine structure to be the sole purview of the architect; the larger forms can be left to patterns
and their application by the inhabitants. Design is ever ongoing not only as we add a new
room to a house, but as we are attentive to repainting, replacing worn carpets, or upgrad-
ing the kitchen sink. Most arts echo analogous sentiments. In our search for others who
ascribe God’s home as being in the details, we find ourselves in the good company of the
19th century French author Gustav Flaubert. The French poet Paul Valery advises us that a
poem is never done and bears continual rework, and to stop working on it is abandonment.
Such preoccupation with detail is common to all endeavors of excellence. So maybe there
is little new here, but in reading this book you will be challenged to take up good disci-
plines that you long ago surrendered to apathy or a desire for spontaneity and just
“responding to change.”
      Unfortunately, we usually don’t view such concerns as key cornerstones of the art of
programming. We abandon our code early, not because it is done, but because our value
system focuses more on outward appearance than on the substance of what we deliver.
```

slides.title: Foreword — PDF page 22
slides.body:
```text
xxii                                                                               Foreword


This inattentiveness costs us in the end: A bad penny always shows up. Research, neither in
industry nor in academia, humbles itself to the lowly station of keeping code clean. Back
in my days working in the Bell Labs Software Production Research organization (Produc-
tion, indeed!) we had some back-of-the-envelope findings that suggested that consistent
indentation style was one of the most statistically significant indicators of low bug density.
We want it to be that architecture or programming language or some other high notion
should be the cause of quality; as people whose supposed professionalism owes to the
mastery of tools and lofty design methods, we feel insulted by the value that those factory-
floor machines, the coders, add through the simple consistent application of an indentation
style. To quote my own book of 17 years ago, such style distinguishes excellence from
mere competence. The Japanese worldview understands the crucial value of the everyday
worker and, more so, of the systems of development that owe to the simple, everyday
actions of those workers. Quality is the result of a million selfless acts of care—not just of
any great method that descends from the heavens. That these acts are simple doesn’t mean
that they are simplistic, and it hardly means that they are easy. They are nonetheless the
fabric of greatness and, more so, of beauty, in any human endeavor. To ignore them is not
yet to be fully human.
     Of course, I am still an advocate of thinking at broader scope, and particularly of the
value of architectural approaches rooted in deep domain knowledge and software usability.
The book isn’t about that—or, at least, it isn’t obviously about that. This book has a subtler
message whose profoundness should not be underappreciated. It fits with the current saw
of the really code-based people like Peter Sommerlad, Kevlin Henney and Giovanni
Asproni. “The code is the design” and “Simple code” are their mantras. While we must
take care to remember that the interface is the program, and that its structures have much
to say about our program structure, it is crucial to continuously adopt the humble stance
that the design lives in the code. And while rework in the manufacturing metaphor leads to
cost, rework in design leads to value. We should view our code as the beautiful articulation
of noble efforts of design—design as a process, not a static endpoint. It’s in the code that
the architectural metrics of coupling and cohesion play out. If you listen to Larry Constan-
tine describe coupling and cohesion, he speaks in terms of code—not lofty abstract con-
cepts that one might find in UML. Richard Gabriel advises us in his essay, “Abstraction
Descant” that abstraction is evil. Code is anti-evil, and clean code is perhaps divine.
     Going back to my little box of Ga-Jol, I think it’s important to note that the Danish
wisdom advises us not just to pay attention to small things, but also to be honest in small
things. This means being honest to the code, honest to our colleagues about the state of our
code and, most of all, being honest with ourselves about our code. Did we Do our Best to
```

```text
2                                                                 Chapter 1: Clean Code


     This is a book about good programming. It is filled with code. We are going to look at
code from every different direction. We’ll look down at it from the top, up at it from the
bottom, and through it from the inside out. By the time we are done, we’re going to know a
lot about code. What’s more, we’ll be able to tell the difference between good code and bad
code. We’ll know how to write good code. And we’ll know how to transform bad code into
good code.


There Will Be Code
One might argue that a book about code is somehow behind the times—that code is no
longer the issue; that we should be concerned about models and requirements instead.
Indeed some have suggested that we are close to the end of code. That soon all code will
be generated instead of written. That programmers simply won’t be needed because busi-
ness people will generate programs from specifications.
     Nonsense! We will never be rid of code, because code represents the details of the
requirements. At some level those details cannot be ignored or abstracted; they have to be
specified. And specifying requirements in such detail that a machine can execute them is
programming. Such a specification is code.
     I expect that the level of abstraction of our languages will continue to increase. I
also expect that the number of domain-specific languages will continue to grow. This
will be a good thing. But it will not eliminate code. Indeed, all the specifications written
in these higher level and domain-specific language will be code! It will still need to
be rigorous, accurate, and so formal and detailed that a machine can understand and
execute it.
     The folks who think that code will one day disappear are like mathematicians who
hope one day to discover a mathematics that does not have to be formal. They are hoping
that one day we will discover a way to create machines that can do what we want rather
than what we say. These machines will have to be able to understand us so well that they
can translate vaguely specified needs into perfectly executing programs that precisely meet
those needs.
     This will never happen. Not even humans, with all their intuition and creativity,
have been able to create successful systems from the vague feelings of their customers.
Indeed, if the discipline of requirements specification has taught us anything, it is that
well-specified requirements are as formal as code and can act as executable tests of that
code!
     Remember that code is really the language in which we ultimately express the require-
ments. We may create languages that are closer to the requirements. We may create tools
that help us parse and assemble those requirements into formal structures. But we will
never eliminate necessary precision—so there will always be code.
```

```text
If you have been a programmer for more than two or three years, you have probably been
```

```text
The Total Cost of Owning a Mess                                                              5


The Grand Redesign in the Sky
Eventually the team rebels. They inform management that they cannot continue to develop
in this odious code base. They demand a redesign. Management does not want to expend
the resources on a whole new redesign of the project, but they cannot deny that productiv-
ity is terrible. Eventually they bend to the demands of the developers and authorize the
grand redesign in the sky.
     A new tiger team is selected. Everyone wants to be on this team because it’s a green-
field project. They get to start over and create something truly beautiful. But only the best
and brightest are chosen for the tiger team. Everyone else must continue to maintain the
current system.
     Now the two teams are in a race. The tiger team must build a new system that does
everything that the old system does. Not only that, they have to keep up with the changes
that are continuously being made to the old system. Management will not replace the old
system until the new system can do everything that the old system does.
     This race can go on for a very long time. I’ve seen it take 10 years. And by the time it’s
done, the original members of the tiger team are long gone, and the current members are
demanding that the new system be redesigned because it’s such a mess.
     If you have experienced even one small part of the story I just told, then you already
know that spending time keeping your code clean is not just cost effective; it’s a matter of
professional survival.

Attitude
Have you ever waded through a mess so grave that it took weeks to do what should have
taken hours? Have you seen what should have been a one-line change, made instead in
hundreds of different modules? These symptoms are all too common.
     Why does this happen to code? Why does good code rot so quickly into bad code? We
have lots of explanations for it. We complain that the requirements changed in ways that
thwart the original design. We bemoan the schedules that were too tight to do things right.
We blather about stupid managers and intolerant customers and useless marketing types
and telephone sanitizers. But the fault, dear Dilbert, is not in our stars, but in ourselves.
We are unprofessional.

requirements? What about the schedule? What about the stupid managers and the useless
marketing types? Don’t they bear some of the blame?
     No. The managers and marketers look to us for the information they need to make
promises and commitments; and even when they don’t look to us, we should not be shy
about telling them what we think. The users look to us to validate the way the requirements
will fit into the system. The project managers look to us to help work out the schedule. We
```

slides.body:
```text
6                                                                                      Chapter 1: Clean Code


are deeply complicit in the planning of the project and share a great deal of the responsi-
bility for any failures; especially if those failures have to do with bad code!
     “But wait!” you say. “If I don’t do what my manager says, I’ll be fired.” Probably not.
Most managers want the truth, even when they don’t act like it. Most managers want good
code, even when they are obsessing about the schedule. They may defend the schedule and
requirements with passion; but that’s their job. It’s your job to defend the code with equal
passion.
     To drive this point home, what if you were a doctor and had a patient who demanded
that you stop all the silly hand-washing in preparation for surgery because it was taking
too much time?2 Clearly the patient is the boss; and yet the doctor should absolutely refuse
to comply. Why? Because the doctor knows more than the patient about the risks of dis-
ease and infection. It would be unprofessional (never mind criminal) for the doctor to
comply with the patient.
     So too it is unprofessional for programmers to bend to the will of managers who don’t
understand the risks of making messes.

The Primal Conundrum
Programmers face a conundrum of basic values. All developers with more than a few years
experience know that previous messes slow them down. And yet all developers feel
the pressure to make messes in order to meet deadlines. In short, they don’t take the time
to go fast!
     True professionals know that the second part of the conundrum is wrong. You will not
make the deadline by making the mess. Indeed, the mess will slow you down instantly, and
will force you to miss the deadline. The only way to make the deadline—the only way to
go fast—is to keep the code as clean as possible at all times.

The Art of Clean Code?
Let’s say you believe that messy code is a significant impediment. Let’s say that you accept
that the only way to go fast is to keep your code clean. Then you must ask yourself: “How
do I write clean code?” It’s no good trying to write clean code if you don’t know what it
means for code to be clean!
     The bad news is that writing clean code is a lot like painting a picture. Most of us
know when a picture is painted well or badly. But being able to recognize good art from
bad does not mean that we know how to paint. So too being able to recognize clean code
from dirty code does not mean that we know how to write clean code!
```

```text
techniques and teachings within are the way that we practice our art. We are willing to
claim that if you follow these teachings, you will enjoy the benefits that we have enjoyed,
and you will learn to write code that is clean and professional. But don’t make the mistake
of thinking that we are somehow “right” in any absolute sense. There are other schools and
other masters that have just as much claim to professionalism as we. It would behoove you
to learn from them as well.

bly not agree with all of them. You might violently disagree with some of them. That’s fine.

authors is that they have readers. Indeed, authors are responsible for communicating well

writing for readers who will judge your effort.

writing it?
```

```text
      Ooops, he’s erasing what he typed!
      He types it again.
      He erases it again!

     ...
     You get the drift. Indeed, the ratio of time spent reading vs. writing is well over 10:1.
We are constantly reading old code as part of the effort to write new code.
     Because this ratio is so high, we want the reading of code to be easy, even if it makes
the writing harder. Of course there’s no way to write code without reading it, so making it
easy to read actually makes it easier to write.
     There is no escape from this logic. You cannot write code if you cannot read the sur-
rounding code. The code you are trying to write today will be hard or easy to write
depending on how hard or easy the surrounding code is to read. So if you want to go fast,
if you want to get done quickly, if you want your code to be easy to write, make it easy to
read.


The Boy Scout Rule
It’s not enough to write the code well. The code has to be kept clean over time. We’ve all
seen code rot and degrade as time passes. So we must take an active role in preventing this
degradation.
      The Boy Scouts of America have a simple rule that we can apply to our profession.

      Leave the campground cleaner than you found it.5

    If we all checked-in our code a little cleaner than when we checked it out, the code
simply could not rot. The cleanup doesn’t have to be something big. Change one variable
name for the better, break up one function that’s a little too large, eliminate one small bit of
duplication, clean up one composite if statement.

passed? Do you believe that any other option is professional? Indeed, isn’t continuous
improvement an intrinsic part of professionalism?
```
